did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a personal promise to Jacob and Israel: the Lord created, formed, and redeemed them, and called them by name to emphasize that they belong to Him.
Water and fire are described as dangers that will not overwhelm Israel, because the Lord is with them and protects them even in difficult circumstances.
The Lord promises to gather Israel from every direction: from the east, the west, the north, and the south.
The verse explains that Israel was created, formed, and made for the Lord’s glory, presenting the nation’s purpose as part of God’s creation.
Israel is called the Lord’s “witness.” Its role is to know, believe, and understand that the Lord is the only God—there was no god formed before Him, and there will be none after Him.
The Lord emphasizes that He alone is the Savior: He foretold it, saved, and proclaimed it, and there is no foreign god among Israel who can claim credit for the salvation.

The Lord is described as the One who makes a way through the sea and a path through mighty waters, recalling the Exodus from Egypt and His ability to lead His people along a seemingly impossible road.

At the heart of the chapter is a declaration about a new act: the Lord will make a way in the wilderness and bring rivers into the desert. Therefore, Israel is called to look toward the future rather than remain focused only on the past.
The criticism of Israel is not focused only on the absence of sacrifices, but on the fact that the people did not truly call on the Lord and burdened Him with their sins and offenses.

Despite Israel’s sins, the Lord declares that He blots out its transgressions for His own sake and does not remember its sins. Forgiveness is presented as an act of divine grace, not as something the people earned themselves.
